newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus president sacks election chief before poll.
newsitem.headline: Belarus president sacks election chief before poll.

text.p: Hardline Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko, seeking extra powers in a referendum on November 24, has sacked the country's top electoral official and warned there will be "war" if the result goes against him.
Lukashenko, 42, announced the sacking during a 2-1/2-hour live address on television on the eve of a vote-catching tour around the former Soviet republic on Friday.

"I have been forced to sign a decree firing Viktor Gonchar. Members of the Central Commission on Elections and Referendums asked me to do this today," the lean, moustachioed president said on state television.
But Gonchar, appointed by parliament in line with the constitution, told Reuters he planned to ignore Lukashenko's decree, which he heard about from the television address.
"This decree is nothing. It's just a sheet of paper. The president is interfering in parliament's powers. I am continuing to carry out my duties," he said by telephone from his office.
Lidiya Yermoshina, a pro-Lukashenko electoral official, was appointed in Gonchar's place, the announcer said later.
Lukashenko is locked in a row with rival institutions which some analysts compare to a 1993 power struggle in Russia which President Boris Yeltsin ended by sending tanks against parliament.

The president warned on Thursday that there would be "war" in Belarus if he lost the referendum. But parliamentary chairman Semyon Sharetsky echoed warnings from Lukashenko's parliamentary opponents, saying the leader was creating a totalitarian state.
"If this draft constitution is put into practice there will be a totalitarian regime in our country with all that entails," Belapan news agency quoted him as saying.
"Sadly, history has already seen this type of regime. For example, there was the fascist regime in Italy, the Hitler regime in Germany, the Franco regime in Spain."

Voters among a population of 10 million in the republic sandwiched between Russia and Poland backed Lukashenko overwhelmingly in July 1994, attracted by his policy of rebuilding a union with Moscow and his vow to fight crime.
Lukashenko is widely seen as having a strong chance of winning the referendum, and he keeps a tight rein on the media.
Russian media said two Russian journalists in Belarus who had criticised him on television could face expulsion.
On Thursday Lukashenko's address was beamed live to hand-picked studio audiences in five regional centres as well as in the capital, where much of his opposition is concentrated.
"I look at my (state-run) television and it is the only sacred screen in the whole of the former Soviet Union," he declared in typically hyperbolic style.

At 7 p.m. local time he began his address, saying two hours later -- when the main evening news was about to start -- that he would continue for another "five or 10 minutes". Instead, the news began 40 minutes late.
Gonchar had infuriated Lukashenko by opposing his bid to extend his powers in a November 24 referendum, describing it as "a piece of legal idiocy" and vowing not to validate the result.

Parliament, the constitutional court and Gonchar's commission which organises and monitors elections say the vote should be advisory and have no constitutional power. But Lukashenko has ignored their rulings, and the existing constitution, by ruling the vote should carry legal force.

If he wins the vote, he will have the right to extend his term by more than two years to November 2001 and to appoint half the electoral commission, half the constitutional court and some of a new, upper house of parliament.
